Arthroscopy is a minimally invasive endoscopic technique in which a rigid fibre-optic arthroscope is introduced into a joint through a small portal to directly visualise the intra-articular structures on a monitor. It is used both diagnostically (to inspect cartilage, menisci, ligaments and synovium) and therapeutically (to repair or resect damaged tissue), most commonly at the knee and shoulder, but also the ankle, hip and wrist. Because it magnifies the joint interior with fluid distension, it allows accurate, targeted surgery through incisions of only a few millimetres, reducing morbidity compared with open arthrotomy.

1Indications — diagnostic & therapeutic

Modern MRI has reduced purely diagnostic arthroscopy, so most procedures are now therapeutic, combining inspection with intervention in a single sitting.

🔬Meniscal tear
Partial meniscectomy or meniscal repair for locking / mechanical knee symptoms
🧵ACL rupture
Arthroscopic ligament reconstruction with hamstring or patellar tendon graft
⚪Loose body
Removal of osteochondral fragment causing locking or catching
🧊Chondral lesion
Debridement, microfracture or cartilage repair of cartilage defects
🧫Synovial biopsy
Sampling / synovectomy in undiagnosed inflammatory or infective arthritis
💪Shoulder pathology
Subacromial decompression, rotator cuff repair, labral (Bankart) repair
Locked knee with true mechanical block→Urgent arthroscopy for bucket-handle meniscal tear
Young athlete, ACL rupture, instability→Arthroscopic reconstruction after rehabilitation of range/strength
2How it is performed
Anaesthesia: usually general anaesthesia; regional (spinal / nerve block) is an alternative, often with post-operative local anaesthetic infiltration.
Positioning & tourniquet: a pneumatic thigh tourniquet provides a bloodless field for knee work; the shoulder is done beach-chair or lateral decubitus.
Portals: small stab incisions (typically anterolateral and anteromedial at the knee) admit the arthroscope and instruments; further portals are added as needed.
Distension: the joint is filled with pressurised sterile saline (or glycine) to expand the cavity, improve the view and wash away debris and blood.
Inspection: a systematic diagnostic sweep of every compartment is performed with the arthroscope before any therapeutic step.
📷 Image placeholder — arthroscopic view of the knee showing femoral condyle, tibial plateau and a probe hooking the medial meniscus.
3Findings & interventions through the scope
Peripheral (red-red zone) meniscal tear in young patient→Meniscal repair (suture) to preserve meniscus
Irreparable central (white-white zone) tear→Partial meniscectomy of the unstable fragment
Full-thickness cartilage defect→Debridement or microfracture to stimulate fibrocartilage
Torn ACL confirmed on probing→Graft passage through drilled femoral and tibial tunnels
Instruments passed down working portals include probes, motorised shavers, radiofrequency ablation tips, punches and suture-passing devices.
Loose bodies are grasped and removed; inflamed synovium can be resected (synovectomy) or sampled for histology and culture.
4Complications, consent & safety
🦠Septic arthritis
Rare but serious joint infection needing washout and antibiotics
🩸Haemarthrosis
Bleeding into the joint causing painful tense swelling
🧬DVT / VTE
Venous thromboembolism; risk-assess and mobilise early
⚡Neurovascular injury
Portal or instrument damage to nerves/vessels (e.g. saphenous nerve)
Consent: discuss infection, bleeding, VTE, nerve/vessel injury, stiffness, recurrence and possible conversion to open surgery.
Anticoagulation & fasting: withhold or bridge anticoagulants per protocol and observe standard pre-operative fasting for anaesthesia.
Tourniquet care: limit inflation time and pressure to avoid nerve palsy, ischaemia and post-tourniquet swelling.
VTE prophylaxis: assess risk and provide mechanical ± pharmacological prophylaxis in line with NICE guidance.
🚩 A hot, swollen, exquisitely painful joint with fever in the days after arthroscopy is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate for urgent Gram stain and culture and arrange emergency washout; delay risks rapid cartilage destruction.
🎓 A true mechanically locked knee (fixed loss of full extension with a springy block) from a bucket-handle meniscal tear is one of the few remaining indications for urgent knee arthroscopy rather than initial conservative management.

Diagnostic laparoscopy is minimal-access endoscopic inspection of the peritoneal cavity and abdominal/pelvic organs. A rigid telescope is passed through the abdominal wall after the cavity is distended with CO₂ (pneumoperitoneum), giving a magnified, illuminated view that lets the surgeon inspect viscera, take biopsies, and often proceed directly to therapeutic intervention in the same sitting.

1Indications — diagnostic and therapeutic
Used when imaging is equivocal and direct visualisation will change management, or to stage disease and access the pelvis. Many diagnostic cases convert to therapeutic in the same anaesthetic.
🔬Acute abdomen
Suspected appendicitis, especially equivocal cases in women of reproductive age
🔬Chronic pelvic pain
Investigate and treat endometriosis, adhesions
🔬Ectopic pregnancy
Diagnose and treat by salpingectomy/salpingotomy
🔬Cancer staging
Detect peritoneal/serosal spread in gastric, pancreatic and gynae malignancy
🔬Ascites / biopsy
Peritoneal biopsy for unexplained ascites or suspected TB/carcinomatosis
🔬Subfertility
Laparoscopy and dye test to assess tubal patency
Equivocal RIF pain in young woman→Laparoscopy inspects appendix AND adnexa in one look
Radiologically resectable gastric/pancreatic cancer→Staging laparoscopy first to exclude occult peritoneal metastases
2How it is performed
Performed under general anaesthesia with the patient supine and catheterised. Entry to the peritoneum is achieved and CO₂ insufflated to create working space.
Entry: closed technique with a Veress needle (usually at the umbilicus), or the safer open Hasson cut-down under direct vision — preferred if adhesions/previous surgery are likely.
Pneumoperitoneum: CO₂ insufflated to ~12–15 mmHg; CO₂ is used because it is non-combustible and highly soluble, minimising embolism risk.
Ports: a 10 mm camera port plus additional 5 mm working trocars sited under direct vision for instruments.
Positioning: Trendelenburg (head-down) shifts bowel out of the pelvis for gynae/appendix work; reverse Trendelenburg aids upper GI access.
📷 Image placeholder — laparoscopic view of the pelvis with camera and working port triangulation after pneumoperitoneum.
3Findings and interventions through the scope
Systematic inspection of the four quadrants, pelvis, peritoneal surfaces and diaphragm. Diagnostic findings frequently trigger a same-sitting therapeutic step.
Inflamed appendix→Proceed to laparoscopic appendicectomy
Endometriotic deposits / adhesions→Ablation/excision or adhesiolysis
Peritoneal nodules or unexplained ascites→Targeted biopsy and peritoneal washings for cytology
Tubal occlusion on dye (chromopertubation)→No spill of methylene blue confirms blocked tube
🎓 Staging laparoscopy can detect low-volume peritoneal metastases invisible on CT, sparing a patient a non-curative open resection — a common exam justification for scoping before major cancer surgery.
4Complications and pre-procedure safety
Most serious complications occur at blind entry. Consent must cover the recognised risks and the possibility of conversion to open surgery.
🩸Visceral injury
Bowel or bladder perforation at Veress/trocar entry
🩸Vascular injury
Aorta/iliac or epigastric vessel damage — potentially catastrophic
💨Gas embolism
Rare CO₂ embolus from intravascular insufflation
🕳️Port-site hernia
Herniation at unclosed 10 mm+ fascial defects
💪Shoulder-tip pain
Residual CO₂ irritating the diaphragm (phrenic, C3–5 referral)
🚫Contraindications
Uncorrected coagulopathy, haemodynamic instability, gross distension
Fasting: standard pre-GA fasting (6 h food, 2 h clear fluids) to reduce aspiration risk.
Coagulation/anticoagulation: check clotting; stop/bridge anticoagulants and assess VTE prophylaxis.
Consent: explicitly include injury to bowel/vessels, bleeding, infection and possible conversion to laparotomy.
🚩 The greatest danger is blind entry injury — perforation of bowel or laceration of a major retroperitoneal vessel (aorta/iliacs). An open Hasson technique is preferred where adhesions or prior surgery raise the risk, and unexplained hypotension after entry demands immediate exclusion of a vascular injury.

Mediastinoscopy is a surgical endoscopic procedure that provides direct access to the mediastinum, usually via a small suprasternal (cervical) incision, allowing the surgeon to advance a rigid scope down the pretracheal plane to visualise and biopsy the paratracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes. It is the historical gold standard for tissue-based mediastinal lymph-node staging in lung cancer and for diagnosing mediastinal lymphadenopathy when less invasive sampling has failed.

1Indications — diagnostic and therapeutic

The overwhelming role is diagnostic and staging tissue acquisition rather than therapy. The commonest indication is nodal staging of non-small-cell lung cancer, where confirming or excluding malignant mediastinal nodes determines resectability.

🔬Lung cancer staging
Biopsy of paratracheal & subcarinal nodes to confirm N2/N3 disease and guide operability
🩺Lymphadenopathy
Diagnosis of unexplained mediastinal nodes or masses, e.g. lymphoma
🫁Sarcoidosis
Non-caseating granuloma sampling when EBUS non-diagnostic
🎯Inaccessible nodes
Nodes out of EBUS/EUS reach or where large-volume tissue is required
Enlarged N2/N3 nodes on CT/PET→Tissue confirmation before deciding on surgery vs chemoradiotherapy
Suspected lymphoma→Large architectural biopsy needed — needle aspiration often insufficient
2Relationship to EBUS-TBNA

Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) is now the recommended first-line, minimally invasive test for mediastinal staging in most units. Mediastinoscopy has become a second-line, confirmatory procedure.

EBUS first: bronchoscopic, no incision, samples paratracheal and hilar nodes with real-time ultrasound guidance.
Mediastinoscopy after: used when EBUS is negative but suspicion remains, when nodes are inaccessible to the needle, or when a larger tissue block is required (e.g. lymphoma subtyping).
EBUS-TBNA negative but high pre-test probability→Proceed to confirmatory mediastinoscopy before curative resection
3How it is performed

Performed under general anaesthesia with the patient supine, neck extended and a sandbag between the shoulders. A short transverse incision is made just above the suprasternal notch.

The strap muscles are separated and the pretracheal fascia is opened.
Blunt finger and instrument dissection develops the pretracheal plane down towards the carina, keeping directly on the anterior tracheal wall.
The mediastinoscope is advanced along this plane; paratracheal (stations 2R/2L, 4R/4L) and subcarinal (station 7) nodes are identified.
Structures are gently aspirated with a needle first to exclude a vessel before biopsy forceps take the node sample.

🎓 The dissection stays strictly in the pretracheal plane on the anterior tracheal wall — straying anteriorly or laterally risks the great vessels; straying too far right endangers the azygos vein and the right main bronchus.
4Complications & pre-procedure safety

Mediastinoscopy is generally safe in experienced hands but sits among high-risk vascular territory, so consent, coagulation status and fasting must be checked beforehand.

🩸Major haemorrhage
Injury to great vessels (aortic arch, innominate/brachiocephalic artery, azygos, PA) — may need sternotomy
🗣️Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Left RLN injury causing hoarseness / vocal cord palsy
🫁Pneumothorax
Breach of pleura during dissection — may need a chest drain
⚠️Airway / oesophagus
Tracheal or oesophageal injury; wound infection is uncommon
On anticoagulant / antiplatelet→Stop and bridge per protocol; check clotting before GA
Fasting for general anaesthesia→Nil by mouth 6 h solids / 2 h clear fluids to reduce aspiration risk
🚩 The feared complication is catastrophic haemorrhage from a great vessel (aortic arch, innominate/brachiocephalic artery or azygos vein). Always needle-aspirate a structure before biopsy, and be prepared for emergency median sternotomy to control bleeding.
